title: Lombardic versals in colour
subtitle: Building large display capitals in two strokes with coloured gouache
excerpt: Lombardic versals are built letters: each stem and curve is made in two separate nib strokes that outline the form, with the outline filled in wet immediately after. Writing them in colour uses the same double-stroke technique with calligraphy gouache thinned to ink consistency.
sourceNotes: Edward Johnston, Writing and Illuminating and Lettering (1906), chapter on built capitals and versals: the double-stroke construction method that Johnston codified from medieval manuscript initials. The Lombardic form is the most common initial capital in Western illuminated manuscripts from the eleventh to the fifteenth century.

glossaryTerms.definition: A built display capital letter constructed from two strokes: the first outlines one side of the stroke, the second outlines the other side, and the wet space between is flooded with ink or gouache immediately to form a solid filled letter.

A style of decorated initial capital developed in northern Italian manuscripts in the Romanesque period, characterised by hairline serifs at the stroke ends, round letter bodies with strong contrast between thick strokes and thin hairlines, and often decorated with pen-drawn flourishes or colour-filled negative spaces.

content.text: is not written as a single nib stroke but built from two strokes that outline each element, then flooded between them while still wet. The

uses this construction at large scale, typically 20 to 80 mm tall. In colour, the two outline strokes and the flood are all done in the same gouache mixture. The colour must be thin enough to flow between the outlines without dragging.

items.name: Mitchell Roundhand nib, 0 (broadest)
items.notes: For versals 30 mm and taller. For smaller versals (20-25 mm), a Mitchell 3 works. The nib edges form the outline strokes.

items.name: Calligraphy gouache, in your chosen colour
items.notes: Dilute to the consistency of thin single cream. Too thick: the flood step streaks and pulls. Too thin: the colour bleeds outside the outline.

items.name: Gum arabic, 2-3 drops per 5 ml of gouache
items.notes: Keeps the gouache from spreading outside the outlined area and gives the dried letter a slight sheen.

items.name: Cartridge paper, 220 gsm, or hot-press watercolour paper
items.notes: Smooth, well-sized paper prevents the flood from feathering at the edges of the outline strokes.

content.text: Start with the letter I, the simplest versal. Rule the letter height (aim for 50 mm for a first attempt). Stroke 1: place the nib at the top of the stem with the nib at about 30 degrees from horizontal. Pull downward along the left side of the stem to the baseline. Stroke 2: place the nib at the same top position but shifted 3 to 5 mm to the right. Pull downward parallel to the first stroke, forming the right edge of the stem. The two outline strokes leave a channel between them approximately 3 mm wide. Flood this channel immediately with the nib tip, drawing the loaded nib slowly down the centre of the channel so the wet gouache fills the gap. The flood merges with both outline strokes while they are still slightly wet.

Lombardic versals end in hairline serifs: thin horizontal lines at the head and foot of each stem and curve. After the stem has dried enough to be handled (about 5 minutes), add hairlines with the nib corner at near-0 degrees to the writing line. The serif is one or two fine passes across the stem end, slightly wider than the stem. In colour, the serif is the same colour as the letter body.

Round letters (O, C, D, G, Q) require the same double-stroke approach on the curves. Build the left-hand arc as stroke 1, then return to build the right-hand arc as stroke 2. Flood the arc channel section by section, working from top to bottom. The hairline junctions where arcs meet verticals or horizontal bars are made as separate short strokes added when the main form is dry.

items.symptom: The flood step streaks and leaves a visible line down the centre of the stem
items.cause: The gouache is slightly too thick, or the outline strokes dried too quickly before flooding.
items.fix: Thin the gouache a little further. Work in a slightly cooler or more humid room where the paper stays slightly damp longer.

items.symptom: The colour bleeds past the outline strokes
items.cause: The gouache is too thin, or the paper surface is too absorbent.
items.fix: Add 2 drops of gum arabic to the mixture and try on a different paper (HP watercolour paper rather than cartridge).
